annotations.text:
Butterloom — mobile-first storefront, 390 × 844 phone frames.

Styled from the logo: paper, ink, dot-grey, arched tracked caps, no third colour. Front page carries the anatomy of a large apparel storefront (promo strip, full-bleed hero, category tiles, scroll rail, editorial band); the listing follows the quieter luxury-house pattern (breadcrumb, sticky filter and sort, large imagery, sparse tracked labels). Anatomy only — no other house's marks, faces or copy.

Bracketed items are facts nobody has settled. Product names, prices and the TrxID are sample values.

Lifted off the logo file, not guessed:

paper #f2eee6 · lift #f8f5ef · grid line #eee9e1 (28px)
ink #33383a · secondary #62635c · quiet #6c6b64
hairline #e2ddd1 · field edge #dcd6c9 · dot #a3a194

The quiet ink is NOT the logo's #83827b: that measures 3.33:1 on paper and fails the 4.5:1 floor for small text. #6c6b64 is the same colour walked down to 4.62:1. #a3a194 is for dots and rules only — never text.

Display and body: ui-serif, Georgia — 400 weight, never bold.
Labels, buttons, chrome: system-ui caps, 9.5–11px, .14–.26em tracking.
Radius 2px. Controls 52–54px. No shadows, no gradients except the two image scrims. No webfont, so nothing here reopens that decision.

Front page. Everything here is static markup over pre-generated image derivatives, so the whole page stays edge-cacheable: one round trip from Dhaka.

The rail scrolls on CSS scroll-snap — a big storefront's carousel without a carousel script. The promo strip is a constant, not a per-visitor message, which is what keeps it out of the cache rules.

The cart count is still the only per-visitor pixel on the page, and the logo seal signs off the footer at its full lockup.

Listing. Filter and Sort are real GET forms — the URL carries them, so every filtered view is its own cacheable page. Chips are the applied parameters, removable.

Load the next six is a link to page two, not infinite scroll: nothing to hydrate, and the crawler follows it.

No wishlist heart. It would need either an account (there is none) or state outside the 1–2KB JS budget, so the pattern is left out rather than faked.

Still no stock line anywhere — that is what lets this page be cached at all.

Product. The three accordions are native <details> — zero script, and they collapse the page to one screen of decision instead of three of prose.

The gallery is a CSS scroll-snap row, which fixes the thing the wireframe pass flagged: the old markup stacked every photograph above the price.

Nothing says whether the piece is in stock, and nothing should (ADR-0007). Add to cart is the first POST allowed to set a cookie, so it is an uncached path.

Cart. Uncached and cookie-keyed, so this page may carry per-visitor truth without the caching rules biting.

The − and + are real submit buttons that POST and redirect; quantity needs no JS.

Delivery is priced by our own flat rule — Pathao is never asked for a live quote (ADR-0004).

Checkout. One page, one POST, three numbered movements. Nav is stripped from the header on purpose.

The selects work: city → zone → area, the cascade ADR-0004 makes mandatory, each step standing in for a fetch of one edge-cacheable option fragment rather than shipping the whole location tree.

The bKash reveal is CSS :has(), not script. Total JS on this screen is the cascade and the cart badge — nothing else.

The same screen with JavaScript off — the hard requirement, drawn rather than assumed.

Each Load button is a real submit; the page comes back with the next list filled in and the earlier answers kept. Two extra round trips from Dhaka, where the enhanced path costs none.

On the shop pages this visitor also loses the cart count, because that badge is the other half of the JS budget.

Option B, kept so the choice is on the table — not the recommendation.

For: three short screens read better on a phone, a mistake is cheaper to recover, and the JS-off path stops being a second path.

Against: two or three extra round trips from Dhaka on every checkout, which is the cost ADR-0007 spends the whole architecture avoiding, and a form that can be abandoned in three places instead of one.
